description: What makes one password stronger than another?
explanation: Length and unpredictability matter most. A long passphrase of unrelated words beats a short password with a few symbol substitutions.
choice0: Replacing letters with lookalike numbers and symbols
choice1: Being long and hard to predict
choice2: Changing it every week
choice3: Containing your initials and birth year

description: Why is reusing one password across several sites risky?
explanation: If any one site is breached, attackers try the same address and password everywhere else, and every reused account falls at once.
choice0: One breached site exposes every account sharing that password
choice1: Websites can detect reuse and lock the account
choice2: Reused passwords expire sooner
choice3: It slows down the login process

description: What does a password manager do?
explanation: It generates and stores a different strong password for every site, so you only have to remember one master password.
choice0: Sends your passwords to the sites you visit automatically
choice1: Replaces the need for any password at all
choice2: Generates and stores a unique strong password for every site
choice3: Encrypts your internet connection

description: What does multi-factor authentication add beyond a password?
explanation: It requires a second, separate proof of identity, so a stolen password alone is not enough to get in.
choice0: A second, separate proof of identity
choice1: A longer password
choice2: An encrypted connection to the website
choice3: A backup copy of your account

description: Which of these is an example of a second factor?
explanation: A one-time code from an app is something you have, distinct from the password you know.
choice0: A longer version of your password
choice1: A security question about your first pet
choice2: Your username
choice3: A one-time code from an authenticator app

description: The three classic authentication factors are something you know, something you have, and what?
explanation: The third is something you are: a biometric such as a fingerprint or face.
choice0: Something you remember
choice1: Something you are
choice2: Something you wrote down
choice3: Something you bought

description: What is phishing?
explanation: Phishing is a message designed to trick you into giving up credentials or clicking something harmful, usually by impersonating someone you trust.
choice0: A way of listening to network traffic
choice1: A method of guessing passwords automatically
choice2: A message impersonating someone you trust to steal credentials or spread malware
choice3: A type of firewall rule

description: Which is the strongest warning sign in an email?
explanation: Urgency combined with an unexpected request to log in through a supplied link is the standard phishing pattern.
choice0: Urgent pressure plus a link asking you to log in
choice1: The message contains an attachment
choice2: The message was sent in the evening
choice3: The message addresses you by name

description: An email from your bank asks you to confirm your password by replying. What should you conclude?
explanation: Legitimate organisations never ask for your password. Any message that does is fraudulent.
choice0: It is genuine if the logo looks right
choice1: It is fraudulent, because real organisations never ask for your password
choice2: It is genuine if it arrived in your inbox rather than spam
choice3: It is genuine if the sender name matches the bank

description: What is the safest way to reach your bank after a suspicious message?
explanation: Ignore the message and go to the site yourself using a known address or the official app, so no supplied link is involved.
choice0: Click the link but check the padlock first
choice1: Reply asking whether the message is genuine
choice2: Forward it to a colleague for a second opinion and then click
choice3: Ignore the message and open the site yourself from a known address

description: What is spear phishing?
explanation: Spear phishing is targeted: the message uses details about you or your organisation to be far more convincing.
choice0: A targeted message using real details about you to be convincing
choice1: Phishing sent to millions of addresses at once
choice2: Phishing carried out over the telephone
choice3: A phishing message with an attachment

description: What is malware?
explanation: Malware is any software written to damage, disrupt or gain unauthorised access to a system.
choice0: Software that has become out of date
choice1: Software written to damage, disrupt or gain unauthorised access
choice2: Software that runs slowly
choice3: Software installed without a licence

description: What does ransomware do?
explanation: Ransomware encrypts your files and demands payment for the key to unlock them.
choice0: Records everything you type
choice1: Shows unwanted advertisements
choice2: Encrypts your files and demands payment to restore them
choice3: Slowly deletes your operating system

description: What does spyware do?
explanation: Spyware secretly gathers information about you and sends it to someone else.
choice0: Secretly collects information about you and sends it elsewhere
choice1: Encrypts files for ransom
choice2: Blocks access to websites
choice3: Speeds up your computer by removing files

description: What is a trojan?
explanation: A trojan looks like something useful so you install it willingly, while it does something harmful in the background.
choice0: Malware that spreads without any user action
choice1: A tool for scanning networks
choice2: A type of firewall
choice3: Malware disguised as something useful so you install it yourself

description: Why is the best defence against ransomware a good backup?
explanation: If you can restore your files from a clean, separate backup, the attackers leverage disappears.
choice0: Because backups prevent the infection occurring
choice1: Because you can restore your files instead of paying
choice2: Because backups alert you to the attack
choice3: Because ransomware cannot encrypt backed-up files

description: Why does installing software updates promptly matter for security?
explanation: Updates close known vulnerabilities. Once a flaw is public, unpatched systems are the easiest targets.
choice0: They close known flaws that attackers are already exploiting
choice1: They make the software run faster
choice2: They reset all your passwords
choice3: They remove old files to save space

description: What is a security patch?
explanation: A patch is an update issued specifically to fix a security flaw in software.
choice0: A physical device that protects a computer
choice1: A password that expires quickly
choice2: An update issued to fix a security flaw
choice3: A backup taken before an upgrade

description: What does HTTPS provide that HTTP does not?
explanation: HTTPS encrypts the traffic between you and the site, so it cannot be read or altered along the way.
choice0: A faster connection
choice1: Encryption of the traffic between you and the site
choice2: A guarantee that the site is trustworthy
choice3: Protection against viruses on the site

description: Does the padlock in the address bar mean a website is safe to trust?
explanation: It only means the connection is encrypted. A criminal can obtain a certificate for their own fraudulent site.
choice0: Yes, it means the site has been verified as legitimate
choice1: Yes, it means the site is scanned for malware
choice2: Yes, it guarantees the owner is a registered company
choice3: No, it only means the connection is encrypted

description: What is the risk of using public wi-fi for sensitive work?
explanation: Others on the network, or a fake hotspot, may be able to intercept or interfere with your traffic.
choice0: Others on the network may intercept or interfere with your traffic
choice1: The connection uses more battery
choice2: Websites load in a different language
choice3: Your device will be automatically infected

description: What does a VPN do on an untrusted network?
explanation: It encrypts your traffic in a tunnel to a server you choose, so the local network cannot read it.
choice0: Makes your device invisible to all attacks
choice1: Encrypts your traffic so the local network cannot read it
choice2: Removes malware already on your device
choice3: Blocks all phishing emails

description: What is a firewall?
explanation: A firewall controls which network traffic is allowed in or out, according to rules.
choice0: Software that removes viruses from files
choice1: A backup system for network data
choice2: A control that allows or blocks network traffic by rule
choice3: A device that speeds up your internet connection

description: What does the C in the CIA triad stand for?
explanation: Confidentiality: information is available only to those authorised to see it.
choice0: Confidentiality
choice1: Continuity
choice2: Compliance
choice3: Certification

description: What does integrity mean in the CIA triad?
explanation: Integrity means the information is accurate and has not been altered without authorisation.
choice0: The data is kept secret
choice1: The data is accurate and has not been altered without authorisation
choice2: The data is backed up regularly
choice3: The data belongs to the right department

description: What does availability mean in the CIA triad?
explanation: Availability means the information and systems are usable when they are needed.
choice0: Only authorised people can read the data
choice1: The data has not been tampered with
choice2: The data is stored in more than one country
choice3: The information and systems are usable when needed

description: What is encryption, in plain terms?
explanation: Encryption scrambles data so only someone with the right key can read it.
choice0: Scrambling data so only someone with the key can read it
choice1: Compressing data so it takes less space
choice2: Copying data to a second location
choice3: Deleting data so it cannot be recovered

description: What is the point of encrypting a laptops hard drive?
explanation: If the laptop is lost or stolen, the data on it stays unreadable without the key.
choice0: It stops malware from running
choice1: It prevents the laptop from being stolen
choice2: It keeps the data unreadable if the device is lost or stolen
choice3: It speeds up the disk

description: What is personally identifiable information?
explanation: It is information that can identify a specific individual, either on its own or combined with other data.
choice0: Any information stored on a personal device
choice1: Information that can identify a specific person
choice2: Information owned by an individual rather than a company
choice3: Information that has been encrypted

description: What does the principle of least privilege mean?
explanation: Each person and system gets only the access needed to do their job, and no more.
choice0: Give only the access needed for the job, and no more
choice1: Give everyone the same level of access
choice2: Give administrators access to everything
choice3: Remove access from anyone who has not used it recently

description: Why should everyday work be done from a non-administrator account?
explanation: If malware runs under a limited account it can do far less damage than under an account with full control.
choice0: Administrator accounts run software more slowly
choice1: Malware running under a limited account can do far less damage
choice2: Non-administrator accounts cannot be phished
choice3: It reduces the number of passwords needed

description: What should happen to an employees accounts the day they leave?
explanation: Access should be revoked immediately, since dormant accounts are a common route back into a system.
choice0: They should be left active in case they return
choice1: They should be shared with their replacement
choice2: They should be revoked immediately
choice3: They should be renamed and kept for records

description: What is social engineering?
explanation: Social engineering manipulates people into giving up access or information, rather than attacking the technology.
choice0: Manipulating people into giving up access or information
choice1: Studying how social networks are built
choice2: Analysing network traffic patterns
choice3: Designing systems that are easy to use

description: What is tailgating in a physical security context?
explanation: Tailgating is following an authorised person through a secure door without badging in yourself.
choice0: Monitoring someone from a nearby vehicle
choice1: Sending repeated messages until someone replies
choice2: Copying an access badge electronically
choice3: Following someone through a secure door without badging in

description: Someone calls claiming to be from IT and asks for your password to fix an issue. What should you do?
explanation: Refuse, and verify through a channel you already trust. Real IT staff do not need your password.
choice0: Give it if they know your name and department
choice1: Refuse, and verify through a channel you already trust
choice2: Give it if the caller ID matches an internal number
choice3: Give a slightly altered version to test them

description: What is shoulder surfing?
explanation: Shoulder surfing is simply watching someone enter a password or read sensitive information.
choice0: Watching someone enter a password or read sensitive data
choice1: Intercepting wireless network traffic
choice2: Guessing a password from personal details
choice3: Following someone into a building

description: Why does a screen lock matter on a phone or laptop?
explanation: It stops anyone with brief physical access from reading your data or acting as you.
choice0: It saves battery
choice1: It prevents malware installing itself
choice2: It stops anyone with brief physical access from using the device as you
choice3: It encrypts your network traffic

description: Why is it risky to plug in a USB stick you found?
explanation: It may carry malware, or be built to attack the machine as soon as it is connected.
choice0: It may carry malware or be built to attack the machine on contact
choice1: It may use too much power
choice2: It may be formatted incorrectly
choice3: It may overwrite your files by accident

description: Why should you install apps only from official stores or vendor sites?
explanation: Unofficial copies are a common way to distribute malware bundled inside apparently normal software.
choice0: Because unofficial versions are always older
choice1: Because unofficial copies are a common way to distribute malware
choice2: Because official stores are cheaper
choice3: Because unofficial apps cannot be uninstalled

description: What does the 3-2-1 backup guideline suggest?
explanation: Keep three copies of your data, on two different kinds of media, with one of them off-site.
choice0: Back up three times a day for two weeks
choice1: Keep three passwords for two accounts
choice2: Restore within three hours using two people
choice3: Keep three copies, on two types of media, one of them off-site

description: Why should you occasionally test restoring from a backup?
explanation: A backup nobody has ever restored may be incomplete or corrupt, and you find out at the worst possible moment.
choice0: An untested backup may be incomplete or corrupt when you finally need it
choice1: Testing makes future backups faster
choice2: It is required before encrypting a disk
choice3: It frees up storage space

description: You think you clicked a phishing link. What is the best first step?
explanation: Report it immediately. Fast reporting limits the damage, and hiding it only gives the attacker more time.
choice0: Delete the email and say nothing
choice1: Report it immediately so the response can begin
choice2: Change one password and carry on
choice3: Wait to see whether anything bad happens

description: Why does a culture of blaming people for clicking links make an organisation less secure?
explanation: People hide their mistakes, so incidents are discovered late, when the damage is far greater.
choice0: People hide mistakes, so incidents are found much later
choice1: It makes training sessions longer
choice2: It increases the number of phishing emails received
choice3: It has no effect on security

description: What is a vulnerability?
explanation: A vulnerability is a weakness in a system that could be exploited to cause harm.
choice0: An attack that has already succeeded
choice1: A piece of malicious software
choice2: A weakness that could be exploited to cause harm
choice3: A rule that blocks network traffic

description: What is the difference between a threat and a vulnerability?
explanation: A threat is something that could cause harm; a vulnerability is the weakness it would exploit.
choice0: A threat is what could cause harm, a vulnerability is the weakness it exploits
choice1: A threat is internal, a vulnerability is external
choice2: They mean the same thing
choice3: A threat is technical, a vulnerability is human

description: What is a data breach?
explanation: A data breach is an incident in which information is accessed or disclosed without authorisation.
choice0: Any failure of a computer system
choice1: An incident where information is accessed or disclosed without authorisation
choice2: A backup that could not be restored
choice3: A password that has expired

description: What should make you cautious about a website address like paypa1-secure-login.com?
explanation: The domain is not the real one. Lookalike characters and extra words are how fraudulent sites imitate real ones.
choice0: The domain is a lookalike, not the real organisations address
choice1: The address is too long to be genuine
choice2: It uses hyphens, which are not allowed
choice3: It ends in .com rather than .org

description: Which part of a web address determines which site you are actually visiting?
explanation: The domain immediately before the first single slash is the real destination; anything after it is controlled by that site.
choice0: The first word after https
choice1: The text at the very end of the address
choice2: The domain just before the first single slash
choice3: Any part containing the organisations name

description: Why are browser extensions worth being cautious about?
explanation: Extensions can often read and change everything you do in the browser, so a malicious or hijacked one is very powerful.
choice0: They always slow the browser down significantly
choice1: They can often read and change everything you do in the browser
choice2: They prevent updates from installing
choice3: They disable the padlock indicator

description: Why is security described as a process rather than a product?
explanation: Threats, systems and people keep changing, so protection must be maintained continuously rather than installed once.
choice0: Because security software must be bought by subscription
choice1: Because no product has ever worked
choice2: Because it is handled by a dedicated team
choice3: Because threats and systems keep changing, so it must be maintained continuously
